title: Agentic Commerce Trends: How AI Is Changing the Way We Buy
summary: Explore agentic commerce trends, adoption barriers and growth opportunities. See how AI-led discovery, checkout and repeat purchases could affect merchants.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


A user types “buy my regular groceries, less than ₹2,000” into an AI assistant. In a supported flow, the assistant will find the items, review prices, fill the basket and help the user pay. The user does not have to visit a merchant website if in-chat checkout is supported. Payment still requires customer approval or valid pre-authorisation.


That is agentic commerce. Payment systems, regulators and merchants are competing to develop infrastructure for agentic commerce to grow.


What does the future of agentic commerce look like? How rapidly is this growing, and what should your business be doing about it today?


### Key Takeaways


- Agentic commerce trends point towards conversational checkout, verifiable permissions and better agent identity.
- AI-assisted product discovery and delegated purchasing are different stages of adoption.
- Trust, liability, fraud and interoperability remain significant agentic commerce challenges.
- New sales channels and repeat purchases offer opportunities, but merchants should measure completed orders and customer outcomes.


##


What Is Agentic Commerce?


[Agentic commerce](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-agentic-commerce/) is when an AI agent handles the process of buying. The customer establishes the objective, the budget, and the rules. The agent searches for products based on these parameters, selects the product(s), and makes the payment(s) within the authority and payment flow available to it.


##


The Current State of Agentic Commerce Adoption


[McKinsey estimates](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-agentic-commerce-opportunity-how-ai-agents-are-ushering-in-a-new-era-for-consumers-and-merchants) that agentic commerce could orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global retail sales by 2030, including $900 billion to $1 trillion in US B2C retail. These projections cover goods, excluding services and B2B. They describe a potential market, rather than sales already completed by agents.


Users are increasingly beginning their search processes with AI tools. Product discovery, AI-assisted checkout and autonomous purchasing are different stages of adoption; interest in one does not establish use of all three.


In India, we’re seeing rapid growth in the development of agentic commerce. For instance, in October 2025, we[announced Agentic Payments](https://www.cashfree.com/news-room/cashfree-payments-becomes-one-of-the-first-fintechs-in-india-to-unveil-agentic-payments-bringing-end-to-end-ai-commerce-inside-chat/) , allowing users to complete purchases directly through a supported chat interface. UPI’s delegation and pre-authorisation capabilities are also relevant, but availability and customer approval depend on the specific flow.


##


Three Models Shaping Agentic Commerce


Three emerging models describe how agents may engage with your business. Each of these models will ask different things from you as a merchant.


**Agent to site** : The customer’s agent comes to your site, looks at your catalog and checks out. For many businesses, this is where the experience begins.


**Agent to agent:** The customer’s agent negotiates with your commerce agent. The two agents work together to agree upon a purchase or other action and they may finalize the order within permissions set by the humans involved.


**Brokered agent to site** : An intermediary system handles interactions across multiple agents and sites. As a merchant, you become part of a broader process, the details of which the broker controls.


These models are still evolving. Merchants may encounter more than one, so the commercial opportunity depends on where their customers shop and how those agents reach the business.


##


Agentic Commerce Trends to Watch


Five agentic commerce trends are changing how customers discover products, reach checkout and approve payments.


### 1. The Checkout Process Is Moving into the Conversation


Checkout can now be completed inside a supported conversation interface. This means discovery, decision-making and payment can occur in the same space. For merchants, the opportunity is to carry purchase intent through to a paid order. Measure how many customers complete payment after an in-chat recommendation.


### 2. Open Protocols Are Defining Different Parts of the Journey


Examples include:


- **Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP)** : OpenAI and Stripe’s protocol supports shopping and checkout experiences inside ChatGPT and other compatible agents.
- **Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)** : Google-initiated AP2 is focused on facilitating delegated payment authorization while including a verifiable audit trail.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** : MCP provides the ability to connect AI-based applications to external systems.
- **WebMCP** : WebMCP is an emerging standard specifically designed for web applications. It allows for direct exposure of website actions to browser agents. It serves a different interface layer from MCP.


These standards address different parts of the journey. Compatibility with one protocol does not guarantee distribution across every AI platform. Merchants should assess which platforms their customers use and which commerce integrations those platforms accept.


### 3. UPI Is Supporting More Controlled Payment Flows


UPI currently has components needed to support delegated payments. Specifically:


- **Reserve Pay** : Allows customers to block funds once for multiple subsequent payments to a specific merchant, subject to the approved terms.
- **UPI Circle** : Enables a primary user to authorize secondary users to initiate payments on their behalf. NPCI also describes linked software/device flows, with limits and user consent.


These capabilities do not make every UPI payment autonomous. In our WebMCP QR checkout, the user scans the QR code and approves the payment. Our[agentic UPI guide](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/agentic-upi-payments-in-india/) explains how that differs from valid pre-authorisation. The opportunity is to simplify repeat purchases where the chosen flow supports it, while keeping spending permissions clear to the customer.


### 4. Agent Identity Is Becoming a Trust Requirement


Customer, order and transaction IDs do not by themselves establish an agent’s identity or authority. Card networks are developing ways for merchants to recognise agents and understand their instructions. For example,[Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol](https://developer.visa.com/docs/trusted-agent-protocol) uses message signatures to help merchants verify agents and their intent.


For merchants, this addresses a practical problem: recognising legitimate agent traffic while keeping malicious bots out. Blocking all automation could also block a potential customer’s shopping assistant.


### 5. Repeat Purchases Offer a Natural Starting Point


Subscriptions, bill payments and loan repayments are predictable, which makes them a natural fit for early agentic payment where the required permissions and payment support exist. Low-value/repetitive purchases such as groceries and daily essentials are also possible use cases. Existing[recurring payments](https://www.cashfree.com/recurring-payment/) do not automatically become agentic: an agent adds decision-making within the customer’s permitted scope. Its value could come from adjusting a grocery basket to price and availability, rather than simply repeating a scheduled debit.


##


Agentic Commerce Adoption: How Ready Are Shoppers?


There’s plenty of interest in using artificial intelligence (AI) in shopping; however, trust is much lower than enthusiasm would suggest.


[Riskified’s Q1 2026 survey](https://www.riskified.com/press/riskified-agentic-commerce-pulse/) of 2,000 US and UK consumers illustrates the gap between interest and trust. While 61.5 percent had used AI for product discovery and recommendations, 55 percent were uncomfortable allowing AI agents to make purchases for them. Meanwhile, 73.9 percent expected strong safeguards such as biometrics or one-time passwords. These findings describe the surveyed US and UK consumers, rather than Indian adoption.


### Reading Agentic Commerce Adoption Signals


**Signal** **What it tells merchants** **What it does not establish**


AI-assisted product discovery Shoppers are using AI to compare and shortlist products That an agent completed the purchase


Agent-assisted checkout An agent helped a customer reach payment That payment was approved without the customer


Delegated repeat purchases A supported flow can operate within approved permissions Unlimited authority across merchants or payment methods


##


Agentic Commerce Challenges That Could Slow Adoption


Adoption depends on solving problems that appear when software makes decisions involving a customer’s money.


### Consumer Consent and Trust


Every agent-initiated payment needs clear evidence of customer approval or valid pre-authorisation. Broad permission to “do my shopping” can leave important details unclear, including the merchant, amount, substitutions and expiry of that permission. Customers need to understand what they have authorised.


### Liability and Accountability


If an agent orders the wrong product or exceeds its authority, customers need a clear route to resolve the issue. In the same Q1 2026 survey, 50.8 percent of respondents believed the AI platform should bear responsibility for unauthorised or erroneous purchases. That is a consumer expectation, rather than a legal rule assigning liability. Merchants and platforms need clear responsibilities and records of what was approved.


### Detecting Fraudulent Activity


Historically,[anti-fraud](https://www.cashfree.com/risk-shield-payment-gateway/) and anti-money-laundering (AML) systems have relied on patterns of human behaviour. Agents may browse and act differently. The challenge is to recognise authorised agents while detecting rogue or hijacked agents and suspicious payments. An agent’s verified identity should support risk checks, rather than replace them.


### Resolving Disputes Over Agent Purchases


Agent purchases still need workable refund and[dispute resolution](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-disputes/) processes. A support team may need to establish what the customer approved, what the agent ordered and what the merchant delivered. Approval records and fulfilment evidence answer different parts of that question.


### Evolving Standards and Interoperability


Multiple standards are currently evolving, often addressing different layers rather than directly competing. Examples include ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol), AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol), MCP (Model Context Protocol) and national-level standards. For merchants, the challenge is to assess compatibility without treating every new protocol as a separate rebuild. The relevant question is which interfaces and payment flows their target channels require.


##


Agentic Commerce Opportunities for Merchants


Agentic commerce opportunities are strongest where a new buying experience solves a specific customer problem.


**New sales channels** : Customers are starting buying journeys in AI apps. Merchants can reach them through supported platform integrations or storefronts that agents can access. The useful outcome is incremental completed purchases, rather than visibility alone.


**Less friction at checkout:** Moving payment into a supported conversation can reduce unnecessary handoffs. The opportunity is to complete more purchases without removing the customer’s approval or the payment method’s authentication requirements.


**Better quality of traffic** : An agent may arrive after comparing products and checking a customer’s requirements. That could produce higher-intent visits, but merchants should measure conversion and order value rather than assume a universal uplift.


**Repeat orders at scale** : When a customer establishes rules for an agent, routine orders such as grocery deliveries, subscription renewals, and bill payments can occur on time with less work for each party.


##


Where Merchants Could See Commercial Value


A useful business case connects a shopping request to a confirmed order and measures the cost of completing it. Consider this illustrative Indian grocery purchase at a store that supports agent-led shopping and our desktop WebMCP redirect checkout.


### Example: A Grocery Order Under ₹2,000


A customer asks an AI assistant to buy their usual groceries for less than ₹2,000, with delivery before 6 p.m. The merchant’s shopping integration handles the product and delivery steps; our checkout handles the supported payment interaction.


**Stage** **What the agent does** **Customer or merchant responsibility**


Discovery Compares available products, prices and delivery options The merchant supplies accurate stock, price and delivery information


Order review Prepares a basket within the budget and presents the final total The customer reviews the items, substitutions and delivery choice


Payment Reads the order on the supported checkout and displays the UPI QR code The customer scans the code in their UPI app and approves with their UPI PIN


Confirmation Checks the payment status The merchant confirms payment before releasing the order for fulfilment


The commercial value is a completed purchase with fewer unnecessary handoffs. Measure how many agent-assisted sessions become paid orders, then compare repeat purchases, refunds, disputes and cost per successful order with the usual checkout journey. A rising visit count alone would not demonstrate that value.


Merchants evaluating the systems needed for this journey can use our[agentic commerce readiness checklist](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-agentic-commerce/) , which covers product data, interfaces, payment controls and rollout.

##


Conclusion


Agentic commerce is creating new routes from product discovery to payment, but adoption depends on trust, compatibility and a reliable buying experience. The opportunity for merchants is to turn relevant shopping requests into completed purchases.


Track payment completion, repeat orders, refunds, disputes and cost per successful order. Those outcomes show whether agentic commerce is creating business value, beyond traffic growth or market forecasts.

##


Frequently Asked Questions


#### What does the future look like for agentic commerce?


We expect AI agents to continue searching, comparing and paying on behalf of customers. As an example McKinsey has estimated agentic commerce may be able to orchestrate around $3 trillion to $5 trillion in global retail goods sales by 2030. This is a forecast, not actual completed sales. The development of UPI-based systems in India for eligible delegated payments via AI agents is also progressing, subject to supported flows and approved limits.


#### Will customers still approve agent payments?


Yes, where the flow requires approval for each transaction. Customers approve payments using the same ways we are used to today (OTP/biometric etc). However, for eligible repeat purchases UPI Reserve Pay allows customers to pre-authorize payments up to approved limits for a specific merchant. Our WebMCP QR flow requires the customer to scan and approve each payment.


#### What should businesses measure to understand agentic commerce adoption?


Measure agent-referred visits, completed orders, payment approval rates, repeat purchases, refunds and disputes separately. Product-discovery usage and market-size forecasts are useful signals, but neither measures how many customers have delegated an actual purchase.
